RGX.scope: All 4 rows of data/raw/public_dump/sackmann_archive/wta/wta_matches_2021.csv: 1097 (Muchova d. Petkovic, R128), 1116 (Peterson d. Rogers, R128), 1194 (Zidansek d. Siniakova, R32), 1197 (Badosa d. Bogdan, R32); action exchange_box (all nine counts), exactly as proposed_exchanges.csv.
RGX.reasons: Corrupt beyond doubt: for each match RG's statistics equal Sackmann's two boxes exchanged on all eight shared counts for both players (16 of 16), and not as recorded; RG's MatchBeats (my recount, a second RG record) agrees with RG's statistics; independent records agree too: the hand charts equal RG's serve points, first serves in, aces and double faults for both players of Peterson-Rogers and Zidansek-Siniakova, Court Vision those of Badosa-Bogdan (Bogdan 126 v 127 serve points, the rest equal). The winner is right: RG's winner flag, RG's set scores read from the winner's side equal the row's score (1-6 6-3 6-4, 6-7 7-6 6-2, 0-6 7-6 6-2, 2-6 7-6 6-4), and the row's winner id plays the next round in both Sackmann's rows and RG's documents while the loser's does not, so names and ids go together and are not swapped: only the boxes are. The fix is exact: service games are equal for both players in every match in the row, in MatchBeats and in my score derivation (13-13, 16-16, 13-13, 15-15), so exchanging all nine counts gives RG's box; applied with apply_row_corrections, all four rows read RG's values and pass Stage 0's checks. They are the only differences in 2019-2021 (2,732 of 2,740 linked player rows equal on all eight counts; the other 8 are these).

Test per match: RG's document linked by both names, winner and games; RG's own checks pass; MatchBeats holds no more serve points than RG's statistics; neither MatchBeats nor the key statistics, holding every point, give another split, aces or double faults; no referee holding the player's points reads the row's value on a changing count; the official box passes Stage 0's B0-B9 under the row's score.
W22.reasons: The 6 Oct rule's conditions hold and, for these rows, its reason holds more strongly than at Wimbledon or the US Open: RG's statistics are Sackmann's own Roland Garros record before the fault (2019-2021: 2,732 of 2,740 player rows equal on all eight counts, the 8 being the RGX exchanges, against 98.3-100% for the US Open feed). From 2022 Sackmann's rows come from another record (the one SofaScore shows, per the report and round 1), with a measured fault: second serves booked as first, aces and double faults missed (where they change, the row is lower in 81 of 83 and 182 of 207 player rows), partial or inflated boxes (serve points from 72 short, Kovalik 19 v 91, to 35 over, Nishikori 214 v 179, where MatchBeats holds every point and equals RG, as Court Vision does for Rublev-Daniel). Taking RG's whole box makes RG 2019-2025 one measurement, the one the training data used before 2022, with the nine counts of a match from one source. I therefore apply the source rule, not the 8 Oct bar, to Sackmann's own 2022-2025 rows: the 8 Oct bar asks whether a row of a trusted source is corrupt; here the question is which record is the event's box score, and Sackmann's own history answers it. The evidence on the small differences: where an independent record holds the player's points and a count changes, Court Vision 2022 reads RG's value 237 times and the row's once (first serves in, the excluded matches included), the hand charts 136 and 11; the charts' 11 are their own noise (on sides where RG and the row agree they read the agreed value +1 on 11.9%; on disputed '+1' sides they read the row's 8 of 54). MatchBeats, holding every point, equals RG's break points on all 601 changing rows. The residual risk is on '-1' sides (the row one first serve in below RG): Court Vision reads the row's value once in 20 and the charts twice in 21, above their baselines (0.6%, 1.9%), so RG may be wrong by one on some 5-10% of those sides. I accept it: such an error moves one first serve of a side, unbiased, and is the same kind of error the 2019-2021 training rows carry; the rows it would keep come from the record that is wrong on most of them. Service games: MatchBeats' count (tiebreaks not counted) is right where it changes the row (42 rows, each fitting the score exactly, each equal to my independent derivation from RG's score and MatchBeats' first server); but the proposal also counts the unfinished game of a retirement, which Sackmann's rows never count (62 of 62 retirement rows of 2022-2025), so on 8 matches it would move a correct count by +1. The fallback to the row's count is acceptable: in the 12 matches where MatchBeats lacks points my derivation gives the row's count on all 24 rows, and in the 8 with no MatchBeats file the row's count fits the score exactly.

other_findings: 1. Service games of retirements: the proposal's MatchBeats count (sources._mb_counts, sv_gms_regular: every game with points served by one player) includes the unfinished game at a retirement; Sackmann's rows exclude it (2022-2025: 62 of 62 retirement rows, all 12 with an unfinished game; 2019-2021: 40 of 42). It gives one player +1 in 11 proposed matches (8 of 2022-2025, where Sackmann's count was already right; 3 of 2026). Counting complete games (isGameComplete) fixes it; my values do. With complete games, E1's agreement is 98.1% (2022-2025) and 80.9% (2019-2021), and E3's '56 rows' are 42 corrections, 6 blank counts filled (2023 Q3) and these 8. 2. Service games are fixed by the score and the first server: servers alternate game by game, a tiebreak taking one turn. Derived from RG's score and MatchBeats' first point, they agree with MatchBeats' server on every game it holds in every match of 2019-2026 but 2021 QD029, so they fill the games MatchBeats lacks. They equal the row's count on all 24 rows where the proposal falls back to it, and give Maestrelli-Noguchi (2026 QM080) 14 and 15 where the proposal has blanks. 3. Referee noise baselines (sides where RG and the row agree): hand charts read the agreed first serves in +1 on 11.9%, -1 on 1.9% of 469 sides; Court Vision 2019/2020/2022 +1 1.1%, -1 0.6% of 535. Disputed W22 sides: '+1': charts read the row 8/54, Court Vision 0/63; '-1': charts 2/21, Court Vision 1/20; size 2 or more: charts 1/84, Court Vision 0/160. 4. Court Vision copy: a faulted first serve's row often carries no player ids ('NA': 4,094 rows in RG 2024, 51 in 2022). Reading the point's server off its first row loses those points; reading it off the point's other row, my Court Vision 2022 tallies equal E2's on every cell. 5. stage0_build.apply_box_overrides indexes ov['score'] and ov['minutes'] even when the table has no such columns (KeyError); the proposed table carries both, so it applies, but a table built without them fails (guard with `if col in ov`). 6. Identity slip, outside this vote: 2024 QM126 Kolar d. 'T. Farquhar' (atp 212408, USA) is RG's Thomas Faurel (FRA); RG's box links by the opponent, games and winner, but the row's loser is the wrong player. It needs an identity correction before any box. 7. E6's '252 RG matches without a box get one' counts blank raw rows. By Stage 0's own has_box, 277 matches gain a box: those 252, plus 25 that Stage 0 drops today for failed or partial boxes (14 TML qualifying matches of 2026; 11 of 2022-2025, e.g. Barrios Vera-Kovalik, Uchijima-Yuan, Pigossi-Kawa). 8. TML's RG 2026 main-draw rows (dropped for Sackmann's blank rows) carry the first-serve fault for the men (pooled 64.70% v RG 62.23%; women 63.61% v 63.03%). They should never stand in for Sackmann's rows. 9. Every claim E1-E7 was recomputed from the raw files and holds, with the definitions noted above. My numbers equal the proposal on every class (4,556 player rows) and on 27,149 of 27,162 override values; whole_box_rows.csv otherwise differs from mine only where neither is used: RG's statistics placed on the identity-slip match, 3 hand charts the lead linked in 'equal' matches, one MatchBeats point with scorer '0' (2024 SM123), and service games of non-proposed rows. 10. 2024 men's qualifying: the 4 statistics_short matches and the identity slip keep Sackmann's split, so the pooled first-serve-in rate after the overrides alone is 61.91% against RG's 61.18%. Round 1's split rows of three of those matches, which the candidate keeps, narrow the gap.

addendum.reasons: Test per match (addendum.py): the eight counts already equal RG's statistics (my class 'equal'). The service games come from RG's record: derived from RG's score and MatchBeats' first server, with MatchBeats' server agreeing with the alternation on every game it holds. They sum exactly to the score's completed non-tiebreak games, differ from the row's, and leave the other class tests passed: MatchBeats holds no more serve points than RG's statistics; neither MatchBeats nor the key statistics, holding every point of a player, give another split, aces or double faults; Stage 0's B0-B9 pass with the new service games. The ten Sackmann counts are impossible for the row's own score whichever player served first. In a completed match every completed non-tiebreak game has one server, so the two counts must sum to those games. Eight sum one short (e.g. 19+18 for 38 games), which Stage 0's tolerance of one passes. 2023 SD003 sums 31 for 36, which Stage 0 already drops. 2023 SD048 sums right but splits 13/11, where 24 games without a tiebreak give 12 each whoever served first. TML's zeros are not counts (Stage 0 reads 0 with serve points as missing, rule C25), and Sackmann's three blanks are missing. Filling them from RG's record is the source rule, as for W26's blank main-draw rows; for TML's 2026 rows it is the 6 Oct rule itself. On SM123 the proposal's contradiction rests on one MatchBeats point (set 4, game 10, the first point, Heide serving) with scorer '0', result 'N' and the game score left at 0-0. Counted as lost, it gives Heide 39 first-serve points won against RG's 40. The next point, which Heide won, takes the game to 30-0, so he won that first point too: MatchBeats agrees with RG's statistics, and I skip a point without a scorer.

SVX.scope: All 323 proposed swaps (AO 2025 81; RG 2019 71, 2020 79, 2021 92), in swaps_scope.csv, with the same source rows and match ids as proposed_swaps.csv (323 of 810). My own derivation found exactly these, plus RG 2023 QM119, which I leave out as the lead does: its confirmed override already gives RG's service games, and an exchange applied after the override would undo them.
SVX.reasons: First server proven (svx_truth.py, my decryption and recount): the file's games are in order with no service game holding points of both servers; its first game is set 1 game 1 (set score 1-0 or 0-1 after it); every game it holds is served by the player the alternation names from that game's server, a tiebreak by its first point, earlier sets counted from the row's score; each set it holds whole has the row's games by the games' winners. All 323 pass. The truth comes from the row's score: servers alternate through the match, and a tiebreak takes its turn uncounted (the final set's 10-point tiebreak at 6-6 included). A retirement counts its finished games only; 6 swaps are retirements. Where MatchBeats holds every game, its own count of completed non-tiebreak games equals this truth on 4074 of 4074 proven rows. A second derivation that does not use MatchBeats gives the same truth on all of them: the break identity. A player's service games equal their non-tiebreak games won plus breaks conceded minus breaks made, read off the row's own score and break points. It gives the truth on 323 of 323 swaps and the row as recorded on 0. In two rows (RG 2019 SD010 and SD020) the recorded counts are impossible as they stand: breaks conceded exceed service games, B8. Exchanged, they are consistent. So each row's two counts contradict its own score and break points as well as the point record: corrupt beyond doubt. Exchanging the two counts (exchange_svgms, F2y) gives exactly the truth. It leaves the total, and so B5, unchanged. B8 passes afterwards on every row. No other table of the candidate touches these rows (the decided corrections, round 1's split rows, the RGX exchanges, the RG overrides). The fix is clear, unique and correct. 270 rows read the score as if the winner had served first (the loser did); the other 53 had the winner serving first and read as if the loser had. Links: RG rows by names, winner and games, with RG's player ids equal to MatchBeats'. AO 2025 files by names within tour and round, every winner agreeing with MatchBeats' match winner; the two names short of an exact match are transliterations (Sultanov, Bulgaru).

SVX.notes_for_the_lead: 1. Proof details. A file can lack the opening point of set 1 game 1 (AO 2025 MQ215 first reads 0-30). The set-score field can be wrong after a tiebreak (RG 2021 SD103: 8-6 for 7-6) or empty (the old RG files). AO 2025 leaves 117 game winners as '0'. My proof accepts either the set score after game 1 or its first point as showing the file opens the match, and checks sets by the games' winners. Resting on games and servers, my proven set and swap list equal yours. 2. Five matches you call unproven pass my alternation check (RG 2023 QM073, QM094, QD110; 2025 QM083, QM124). A few you prove fail my order or set checks (e.g. RG 2024 SM116, games out of order; RG 2019 QD087, sets). All of them have the row equal to the truth, so no swap depends on them. 3. The break identity is a second, MatchBeats-free proof. In this round's editions it flags one more swap that MatchBeats cannot prove: AO 2025 WQ230 (7-6(5) 3-6 7-5, row 17/16, identity 16/17). It is not proposed; it could serve the addendum's editions too, where Sackmann's break points are the event's own. 4. RG 2023 QM119 (left out): with Sackmann's own break points the identity backs his 10/11; with RG's (my confirmed override) it backs RG's 11/10. The override is the consistent box, and the exchange must not be applied on top of it.

SVX_addendum2.reasons: The same method and checks as SVX, from my own decryption and recount of the new files (RG 2016-2018 on the API route; 16 codes of RG 2016 have no file on either route): the first server is proven (games in order; the first game is set 1 game 1; every game held follows the alternation, a tiebreak by its first point; each set held whole has the row's games by the games' winners), and the truth comes from the row's own score (a tiebreak takes its turn uncounted; a retirement's finished games only). Where MatchBeats holds every game its own count equals the truth on 1320 of 1320 proven rows. The break identity (service games = non-tiebreak games won + breaks conceded - breaks made, from the row's own score and break points, without MatchBeats) gives the truth on 104 of 105 swaps and the row as recorded on 1. So the rows' two counts contradict their own score and break points as well as the point record, all but 1: corrupt beyond doubt. The exception is RG 2016 SD014 (Stosur d. Halep 7-6(0) 6-3). There the break identity backs the row's 11/10, because the row's break points have Halep losing serve twice where the point record's games show three times. The row's 11/10 needs Halep to have served first. Read that way, the record's game winners, which reproduce the 7-6 6-3 score exactly, would put ten breaks in set 1 alone, against the row's own three in the match. Read with Stosur serving first (every one of its 22 games on the alternation, 17 of 21 service games held), they differ from the row's break points by that one Halep break. The row's service games are the inconsistent count; I confirm the swap. The exchange gives exactly the truth, keeps the total (B5), passes B8 on every row (0 failures after, 0 before), and no other decided table touches these rows: clear, unique and correct. Links: every file paired with its Stage 0 row by names within event, tour and round; on 3 swaps the file's match-winner field does not name the row's winner (RG 2016 SM023 and RG 2018 SM091: the field is missing, '0'; RG 2016 SD070: it names Allertova, though Nara played the next round), while in each the game winners give the row's score from the row winner's side; the names short of an exact match are transliterations or married names, reviewed.

My derivation, made before reading the proposal, found the same rows and values; none added, none dropped. 557 rest on the strict proof; RG 2014 SD078 on the glitch-tolerant reading (a local glitch of at most three records in one set, every other game on the alternation), its truth agreeing with the break identity. Of the fills, 6 (RG 2013-2014: 2013 SD051, 2013 SD061, 2013 SD002, 2014 QD033, 2014 SD010, 2014 SD029) have double faults blank too, so their box stays partial and Stage 0 still drops it (C23) until those are filled; the fill is correct and harmless, but completes nothing.
SVS.reasons: Each set rests on the same proven first server as SVX (my own decryption and recount; the opening of the match shown by the set score after game 1 or by its first point, every game on the alternation, sets checked by the games' winners). The truth is the score's alternation, a tiebreak taking its turn uncounted, a retirement's finished games only. Every set passes the consistency test: each player's non-tiebreak games won equal the truth's service games, less breaks conceded, plus breaks made, from the row's own break points. That makes the new counts the only ones the row's own score and break points allow, independently of the point record. Fills (460): the counts are blank (RG 2013-2014, Sackmann's rows with serve points and no service games) or 0 and 0 with serve points played (RG 2017, which Stage 0 already reads as missing); serve points and break points are present. 'Other' (98): the recorded counts are wrong and not an exchange. 96 have the right total with the split off (87 equal counts where the score forces unequal ones), and two fall short: RG 2023 SM040, 9/9 for 27 games; RG 2024 SM123, 22/22 for 45, the match the overrides leave out for a scorer-less MatchBeats point, here 23/22 as I derived it then. None is a tiebreak counted the other way: no row equals the truth with tiebreak turns added. None of the recorded counts is consistent with its own break points (0 of 98), and every truth is. B5 (the total fits the score) and B8 pass on every set. No set touches a row another table changes: my confirmed overrides, the RGX exchanges, round 1's split rows, the decided corrections or the swaps. Left out, as the proposal does: the RG override matches, and the consistency failures outside them (RG 2026 QM066, RG 2014 SD051).
